plan.topic: Tirzepatide and dehydration on sick days (cold, flu, stomach bug, hot weather): why fluids matter more when appetite and thirst are lower, the label's warning about sudden kidney injury in people who lost fluids through nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea, the everyday signs of dehydration, a calm sick-day checklist, and when to contact a prescriber or get urgent care
plan.angle:
Lane A (log 'lane: A'; publisher adds it to the 'Life on Tirzepatide' playlist). 9–11 min, 14:00 ET, evergreen with no date, holiday or 'this season' words.

Opening: the first spoken sentence answers the title. 'The main dehydration signs to watch for on tirzepatide are feeling thirsty, dark yellow pee, peeing less, and feeling dizzy or tired. They matter most when you're sick and losing fluids.' Then a 'you' scenario: you wake up with a stomach bug and can barely keep water down.

Chapters, named as searched questions:
1. Why does dehydration matter on tirzepatide? Quote the current Zepbound label (rev. 28 Aug 2026) word for word on kidney problems, including sudden (acute) kidney injury, in people who lost fluids through nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea. Copy its exact scope, including any 'some had no known kidney disease' wording, and give no rate the label doesn't print.
2. Why can it creep up? The label's GI side effects and slower stomach emptying in label wording. 'Eating less food also means less water from food' and 'thirst may be easy to miss when appetite is low' are our own untagged lines, worded 'can'.
3. What are the signs of dehydration? The NHS list, copied exactly and tagged NHS.
4. What helps on a sick day? Our own untagged tips: sip fluids little and often unless you've been told to limit fluids; small, bland portions if you can eat. Ask a pharmacist before taking cold, flu or anti-diarrhoea remedies. No product names or doses.
5. What if you have diabetes? The label's higher risk of low blood sugar when tirzepatide is used with insulin or a sulfonylurea, in label wording. 'Ask your prescriber for a written sick-day plan' is untagged.
6. Who should get advice early? Kidney disease, older adults, people on diuretics or blood pressure medicines. Our own 'ask early' line, with no source tag.
7. When should you get help? Vomiting or diarrhoea you can't keep up with, very little or no urine, dizziness or fainting, or confusion → contact your prescriber or healthcare provider right away. Severe or worsening symptoms → 'your local urgent care or emergency number'. Severe stomach pain that won't go away gets the label's pancreatitis instruction, scoped with its own trigger.

Rules:
- Then 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own; ask your prescriber what to do on sick days.' Never mention skipping, delaying or changing a dose.
- No NSAID or GI-bleeding study.
- Re-hook every 45–75 s. One subscribe ask, right after the chapter 4 checklist payoff.
- Every safety line is spoken and also written in full in the on-screen field: the don't-stop line, then 'Not personal advice', then the full prescriber line.
- Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' The publisher puts a ▶ Watch next link to Side Effects on description line 1.
- Thumbnail: state change from worried to answered, 4 words or fewer, not reusing title words (e.g. 'Sick Day Plan'). One labelled calm character holding a water glass, no body imagery.
- Sources: Zepbound PI and Medication Guide (separate URLs), NHS dehydration page with its live review date.

package.description:
Watch for thirst, dark yellow pee, peeing less often, and feeling dizzy or tired, especially on sick days when you're losing fluids. The Zepbound Medication Guide says diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting may cause a loss of fluids (dehydration), which may cause kidney problems.

Contact your prescriber or healthcare provider right away if you have vomiting or diarrhoea you can't keep up with, very little or no urine, or dizziness that won't settle. If you faint, feel confused or unusually drowsy, have trouble breathing, or your symptoms are severe or getting worse, use your local urgent care or emergency number. If you have severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away (listed under pancreatitis), stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away. The Medication Guide says tirzepatide may increase your risk of low blood sugar if used with insulin or a sulfonylurea. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own; ask your prescriber what to do on sick days.

Sources:
Zepbound Prescribing Information (rev. 8/2026): https://uspl.lilly.com/zepbound/zepbound.html#pi
Zepbound Medication Guide (rev. 08/2026): https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/medguide.cfm?setid=487cd7e7-434c-4925-99fa-aa80b1cc776b
NHS, Dehydration: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/dehydration/
Mounjaro Prescribing Information: https://uspl.lilly.com/mounjaro/mounjaro.html#pi

script.hook_pattern: Direct answer first, then a visceral 'you' scenario (3 a.m. stomach bug) with an open loop: the one question to ask your prescriber before you're ever sick

scenes.narration: The main dehydration signs to watch for on tirzepatide are feeling thirsty, dark yellow pee, peeing less, and feeling dizzy or tired. They matter most when you're sick and losing fluids.
scenes.retention_device: Answers the title in the first sentence

scenes.narration: Now picture this. You wake up at three in the morning with a stomach bug. You sip some water, and ten minutes later it's back up.

visual.stock_query: queasy person on couch at night

scenes.narration: You're on tirzepatide, so you're already eating less than you used to. And a small voice asks: is this just a rough night, or should I be worried?
If you've had that thought, it's a sensible one. You're not overreacting, and you're not alone in wondering.
Here's why it's worth asking. The drug's own patient guide says diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting may cause a loss of fluids, and that this may cause kidney problems.
scenes.retention_device: Stakes with a concrete proof point

scenes.narration: The good news? Fluid loss is often something you can spot early and respond to. In the next few minutes you'll get the signs, a calm sick-day checklist, and exactly when to call for help.
And there's one question worth asking your prescriber before you ever get sick. Stay with me, because I'll tell you what it is later on.

scenes.section: Why does dehydration matter on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: Let's start with what the official labelling actually says, because the exact wording matters here.

scenes.section: Why does dehydration matter on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: The Medication Guide for tirzepatide, sold as Zepbound for weight management, says diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting may cause a loss of fluids, called dehydration.

scenes.section: Why does dehydration matter on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: And it says that dehydration may cause kidney problems. Doctors call the sudden kind acute kidney injury. Acute simply means sudden. The kidneys suddenly can't do their filtering job as well as they should.

scenes.section: Why does dehydration matter on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: The label also describes reports from after these medicines reached the market: reports of acute kidney injury, in some cases needing dialysis, in people treated with GLP-1 medicines, including tirzepatide.

scenes.section: Why does dehydration matter on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: And here's the line worth knowing: the label says the majority of those reported events happened in people who had stomach side effects leading to dehydration, such as nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea.

visual.quote: The majority of the reported events occurred in patients who experienced gastrointestinal adverse reactions leading to dehydration such as nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
visual.attribution: Zepbound Prescribing Information, Warnings and Precautions

scenes.section: Why does dehydration matter on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: In plain English, most of those kidney problems came after fluid loss from stomach side effects. That's exactly why the signs in this video matter.

visual.stock_query: stomach cloud, water drop, kidney arrow

scenes.section: Why does dehydration matter on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: The label does give one number. In its two main weight-management trials, acute kidney injury was reported in about five in every thousand people on tirzepatide, compared with about two in every thousand on placebo. And it tells clinicians to check kidney function in people with side effects that could lead to fluid loss, especially when starting or increasing the dose.
scenes.on_screen_text: Kidney injury reported: 5 vs 2 in 1,000 (tirzepatide vs placebo, 2 weight trials, up to 72 weeks)

visual.stat_label: Per 1,000 reported: tirzepatide vs placebo, 2 weight trials

scenes.section: Why does dehydration matter on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: The Medication Guide, the plain-language leaflet for patients, puts it simply: drink fluids to help reduce your chance of dehydration.

scenes.section: Why does dehydration matter on tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: So the label's concern centres on days when fluid is going out faster than it's coming in. But why would that sneak up on you? That's where it gets interesting.

visual.stock_query: leaky water jug being refilled slowly

scenes.narration: Why can dehydration creep up on tirzepatide?
scenes.retention_device: Chapter title as a searched question

scenes.narration: Start with the stomach side effects themselves. They're common, even before any bug arrives.

In the label's two placebo-controlled weight trials, in adults with obesity or overweight, with or without type two diabetes, treated for up to seventy-two weeks, nausea was reported by twenty-five to twenty-nine in every hundred people on tirzepatide, depending on dose. On placebo, it was eight in a hundred.
Diarrhoea: nineteen to twenty-three in a hundred on tirzepatide, versus eight on placebo. Vomiting: eight to thirteen in a hundred, versus two on placebo.

items: Tirzepatide vs placebo, up to 72 weeks

scenes.narration: Put another way, vomiting was reported by roughly one in ten people on tirzepatide, depending on dose. That's someone in a full doctor's waiting room.
scenes.on_screen_text: About 1 in 10 on tirzepatide (8–13 in 100, by dose) vs 2 on placebo

scenes.narration: The label also says tirzepatide delays gastric emptying. In everyday terms, food leaves your stomach more slowly.
Now add two points of our own. These aren't from the label, but they follow common sense.

visual.stock_query: friendly mascot holding up two fingers

scenes.narration: First, food carries water too: soup, fruit, yoghurt. So eating less food can also mean less water from food.

visual.stock_query: small bowl of soup and fruit

scenes.narration: Second, thirst can be easy to miss when appetite is low. If you're not thinking about meals, you may not be thinking about drinks either.
Then comes the illness itself. The NHS lists causes of dehydration including being sick, having diarrhoea, sweating a lot, and having a high temperature.
So a hot day, a flu with a fever, or a stomach bug can stack on top of a smaller appetite. Each one alone might be manageable. Together, they add up.

visual.stock_query: stacking blocks labelled heat fever bug

scenes.narration: Imagine Dana, forty-seven, four months on tirzepatide. It's a hot afternoon, she's been gardening for hours, and she's had half a sandwich all day.
She feels a bit off, but nothing dramatic. So how would she know if it's dehydration? The NHS has a short list, and one item on it is easy to overlook.

scenes.section: What are the signs of dehydration?
scenes.narration: According to the NHS, symptoms of dehydration in adults include feeling thirsty, dark yellow, strong-smelling pee, and peeing less often than usual.

scenes.section: What are the signs of dehydration?
scenes.narration: Also feeling dizzy or lightheaded, feeling tired, a dry mouth, lips and tongue, and sunken eyes.

items: A dry mouth, lips and tongue

scenes.section: What are the signs of dehydration?
scenes.narration: The one that's easy to overlook is peeing less often than usual. You probably don't count bathroom trips, so it can slip by. On a sick day, it's worth noticing.

visual.stock_query: bathroom door with small tally chart

scenes.section: What are the signs of dehydration?
scenes.narration: Here's a tricky part. Feeling tired or a bit dizzy can overlap with an ordinary off day. That's why the pee check helps. It's harder to explain away.

scenes.section: What are the signs of dehydration?
scenes.narration: Two signs together tell you more than one on its own. Dark pee and going less often is a clearer message than just feeling tired.

scenes.section: What are the signs of dehydration?
scenes.narration: Back to Dana. She checks. Her pee is darker than usual, and she realises she hasn't been since lunch. Two signs together, and a cue to act.

visual.stock_query: Dana realising, hand on forehead, indoors

scenes.section: What are the signs of dehydration?
scenes.narration: So what does acting actually look like? Not panic. Not a dramatic fix. Something much calmer.

scenes.section: What helps on a sick day?
scenes.narration: These are practical tips, not the label's words and not personal advice. Your own care team always comes first.

scenes.section: What helps on a sick day?
scenes.narration: One. Sip fluids little and often, unless you've been told to limit fluids. A few mouthfuls every few minutes can be easier than a big glass when your stomach is unsettled.

visual.stock_query: person sipping small glass on sofa

scenes.section: What helps on a sick day?
scenes.narration: If you have been told to limit fluids, for example because of a heart or kidney condition, follow that advice and ask your care team what to do when you're unwell.

visual.stock_query: person on phone to clinic, calm

scenes.section: What helps on a sick day?
scenes.narration: Two. If you can eat, keep portions small and bland. Think toast, crackers, plain rice, or a simple broth.

visual.stock_query: toast crackers and broth on tray

scenes.section: What helps on a sick day?
scenes.narration: Three. Before you take any cold, flu or anti-diarrhoea remedy, ask a pharmacist. Tell them you're on tirzepatide, and mention everything else you take.

scenes.section: What helps on a sick day?
scenes.narration: A pharmacist can also talk you through rehydration drinks and whether one suits you.

scenes.section: What helps on a sick day?
scenes.narration: Four. In hot weather, keep a drink within reach and take shade breaks. Remember, thirst can be easy to miss when you're not hungry.

visual.stock_query: water bottle in shade on bench

scenes.section: What helps on a sick day?
scenes.narration: Five. Keep checking the signs: thirst, pee colour, how often you go, and whether you feel dizzy.

scenes.section: What helps on a sick day?
scenes.narration: Here's the whole checklist in one breath. Sip little and often, unless you've been told to limit fluids. Small, bland portions if you can eat. A pharmacist before any remedy. A drink within reach in the heat. And keep watching the signs.

scenes.section: What helps on a sick day?
scenes.narration: For Dana, that looks like a glass by her chair, small sips through the evening, and some toast. By bedtime she's feeling steadier.

visual.stock_query: Dana relaxed in armchair with water

scenes.section: What helps on a sick day?
scenes.narration: If a calm checklist like this helps, that's what we do here: one tirzepatide question from the research, answered like a friend would. Subscribing means the next answer finds you.

scenes.section: What helps on a sick day?
scenes.narration: But Dana's evening was a mild one. What if you have diabetes too? There's a second thing to watch, and it isn't about water.

scenes.narration: What if you have diabetes?
scenes.retention_device: Chapter title as a searched question

scenes.narration: Tirzepatide is also prescribed for type two diabetes, sold as Mounjaro. And some people taking it for weight have type two diabetes as well.

visual.stock_query: two medicine boxes on clinic table

scenes.narration: The Zepbound Medication Guide says tirzepatide may increase your risk of low blood sugar if it's used with insulin or a sulfonylurea, a type of diabetes tablet.
Signs of low blood sugar listed in the Medication Guide include shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion, a fast heartbeat, and dizziness.
Notice that dizziness shows up on both lists, dehydration and low blood sugar. When you're sick and barely eating, it can be hard to tell what's going on.

visual.stock_query: two overlapping circles with dizzy icon

scenes.retention_device: But here's where it gets tricky

scenes.narration: Which is why this is the question I promised at the start. While you're well, ask your prescriber for a written sick-day plan.

visual.stock_query: person handed written plan at clinic

scenes.retention_device: Pays off the main open loop

scenes.narration: What goes on it is between you and them: what to drink, what to watch, when to check in, and who to call. Stick it on the fridge, so at three a.m. you don't have to think.

visual.stock_query: plan pinned to fridge with magnet

scenes.narration: And it's not only people with diabetes who benefit from asking early. Some people have less room for fluid loss than others.

visual.stock_query: small group of calm people waiting

scenes.retention_device: Open loop: who should ask early

scenes.narration: Who should get advice early?
scenes.retention_device: Chapter title as a searched question

scenes.narration: The NHS says older adults are more at risk, and so are people with diabetes and people taking medicines that make you pee more, called diuretics or water tablets. We'd add two more of our own: kidney disease, and blood pressure medicines. If any of these fit you, ask for advice early, not late.
This isn't a reason to worry. It's a reason to make the call on day one, rather than waiting to see if it passes.
Picture Dana's dad, seventy-eight, also on tirzepatide, plus a water tablet and a blood pressure medicine. For him, a stomach bug means a phone call to his care team on the first day.
And remember that label line: most of the reported kidney problems followed fluid loss from stomach side effects. So even if you're not on this list, the signs still matter.
Which brings us to the most important part of this video: the signs that mean don't wait at all.
When should you get help?

factcheck.summary:
I checked every sourced claim against the live sources (Zepbound PI rev. 8/2026, Zepbound Medication Guide rev. 08/2026, NHS dehydration page last reviewed 01 May 2026, Mounjaro PI rev. August 2026). All the numbers are correct.
- **Kidney injury:** 0.5% vs 0.2% in the pooled Studies 1 and 2, up to 72 weeks, shown as 5 vs 2 in 1,000.
- **Stomach side effects:** nausea 25–29% vs 8%, diarrhoea 19–23% vs 8%, vomiting 8–13% vs 2%.
- **Quotes:** the s13 quote matches the PI word for word, and the s69 quote matches the Medication Guide word for word.
- **Other label lines:** the post-marketing kidney injury and dialysis line, the kidney-monitoring line, delayed gastric emptying, the Medication Guide's 'drink fluids' line and the low-blood-sugar risk with insulin or a sulfonylurea are all stated correctly.
- **NHS:** the symptom list is accurate.

Safety handling is good:
- The pancreatitis stop instruction is limited to its own trigger.
- The don't-switch/stop/change line comes before 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line, and all three are spoken and shown in full.
- People told to limit fluids, and people with heart or kidney conditions, get a caveat.
- Help lines cover all markets.
- Dana is clearly labelled as hypothetical.

The title's promise is paid off.

I found three minor wording issues:
- s61 credits the NHS's 'more at risk' wording with diabetes and diuretics, but the NHS lists those as things that make dehydration more likely.
- s75's recap leaves out 'won't settle' on dizziness, so it reads broader than s67.
- s20's 'with or without type two diabetes' could say more precisely how the two trials differ.

issues.claim: The NHS says older adults are more at risk, and so are people with diabetes and people taking medicines that make you pee more
issues.problem: On the NHS page, only babies, children and older adults are named as 'more at risk'. Diabetes and diuretics appear under 'dehydration is more likely if you…'. The meaning is close, but the attribution is slightly loose.
issues.fix: Replace the narration with: "The NHS says older adults are more at risk, and that dehydration is more likely if you have diabetes or take medicines that make you pee more, called diuretics or water tablets. We'd add two more of our own: kidney disease, and blood pressure medicines. If any of these fit you, ask for advice early, not late."

issues.claim: If you can't keep up with fluid loss, you're barely peeing, or you're dizzy, contact your prescriber right away.
issues.problem: The recap drops the 'won't settle' qualifier from s67, so it's broader than the action list it summarises.
issues.fix: Replace with: "If you can't keep up with fluid loss, you're barely peeing, or you're dizzy and it won't settle, contact your prescriber right away. If you faint, feel confused, or it's severe or getting worse, use your local urgent care or emergency number."

issues.claim: in adults with obesity or overweight, with or without type two diabetes
issues.problem: This is accurate for the pooled data, but the label says Study 1 excluded type 2 diabetes and Study 2 enrolled only people with type 2 diabetes. Saying so gives the exact population.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are legible and on-brand, but #0 best matches the playbook's proven highest-performing format for this niche (state-change before/after, ≤4 words, one simple calm character), with the cleanest contrast and clearest single focal point (the worried-to-calmer face transition). It avoids the slightly alarmist hazard-tape framing of #2 and the two-tier text of #1, while still creating curiosity ("Sick Day Plan" implies there's something you need to know/do). #1 is a solid runner-up with a good curiosity gap, but #2's warning-tape styling edges toward sensationalism the title doesn't fully justify and its kidney mascot is a less immediately readable focal point.

hold_reason:
Packaging check REVISE: The packaging matches the verified script, and nothing in it overclaims, so the verdict is REVISE for two fixable issues.

What's fine:
- **Title:** "Tirzepatide Dehydration: Signs to Watch For" is 43 characters, puts the drug name first and matches the content.
- **Thumbnail:** "SICK DAY PLAN" / "Signs + when to call" is under 4 words, doesn't repeat the title and the video delivers both.
- **Description safety block:** line 1 is empty, as required. The emergency sign is scoped correctly: severe stomach pain that won't go away means stop tirzepatide and call your provider. After that comes the "for anything that isn't one of those emergency signs" don't-stop line. The low-blood-sugar caveat with insulin or a sulfonylurea is there too.
- **Pinned comment:** it copies the script word for word and ends on the exact disclaimer and prescriber line.

What needs fixing:
1. **Description, missing disclaimer (major):** it never carries "Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.", which every caption field must end on.
2. **Description, chapters (minor):** they are an unfinished stub. "MM:SS Why dehydration matters" is literal placeholder text, and with only one real timestamp YouTube won't show chapters. They also leave out the checklist and when-to-get-help sections.

There are no hashtags right now. That's optional, and the fix adds only generic #tirzepatide. Adding the disclaimer after the links keeps the description under 1,250 characters before the first link (about 1,115).

I didn't re-check the science or open the sources, because every packaging claim stays within the verified script. The four sources below are carried over from the content check, which confirmed them; I didn't fetch them again here. (alternative title: Tirzepatide Dehydration: The Sick-Day Signs)
